title: Noll v. eBay, Inc.
lead: Sellers challenged recurring eBay listing charges and settled for automatic account credits or checks. The court approved the class and fund after examining notice, litigation risks, fees, and reduced representative awards.

actors.name: Richard Noll and Rhythm Motor Sports

proceedings: 2011 action narrowed through dismissal motions before discovery, certification motion, and two mediations.
District court approved settlement September 15, 2015 and reduced requested representative payments.
limits: Settlement did not establish liability. User IDs, notice records, and people are different counts; apparent notice coverage is not proof of universal receipt. Fund percentages use different denominators.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Recurring listings produce disputed recurring charges
paragraphs: Richard Noll and Rhythm Motor Sports sold items on eBay using Good ’Til Cancelled listings, renewed every thirty days until ended or sold. Sellers alleged the schedules inadequately disclosed monthly insertion charges and fees for optional features such as bold type or highlighting. They sought disputed renewal fees back.

Before September 16, 2008, the option existed only in Stores, whose schedule expressly described recurring fees. It then entered Core and Motors. Core added express recurring-insertion language in December 2008; Motors and Stores did so in March 2010. Explicit language for both insertion and optional-feature fees followed in June 2012. Differences across markets and dates affected both scope and risk.

The 2011 complaint asserted contract, consumer, unjust-enrichment, fraud, and declaratory theories. Dismissal motions removed foreign entities, repeatedly narrowed fraud theories with amendment allowed, and eliminated an automatic-renewal statutory count with prejudice in 2013. After further pleading, discovery, experts, a certification motion, and two retired-judge mediations, the parties executed a settlement January 14, 2015.

sections.title: The agreement distributes without claim forms
paragraphs: The settlement covered qualifying United States residents and entities paying disputed listing fees: Stores from March 30, 2010, and Core and Motors from September 16, 2008, all through June 19, 2012. Specified court personnel, eBay insiders, and families were excluded.

The $6.4 million fund would automatically credit active accounts and send checks to inactive or closed ones. Expected net payments exceeded $4.5 million, approximately half the relevant first-renewal-month fees. Returned or uncashed residue would go equally to two identified nonprofits rather than eBay. Members released claims arising from the pleaded allegations.

The report counted 1,192,947 unique user IDs, not that many distinct people because one person could hold several accounts. Address processing produced 1,188,451 notice records, another distinct measure.

sections.title: The court certifies for settlement and evaluates actual notice
sections.cue: Shared issues do not erase litigation risks
paragraphs: Judge Edward Davila found Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 satisfied for settlement. Common agreements, schedules, and listing machinery presented central shared questions; representatives suffered the same alleged harm and faced typical defenses, including continued purchases after awareness. Uniform allocation, period coverage, experienced counsel, and investigation supported adequacy. Contract questions predominated, and small claims made separate litigation uneconomical. The court still recognized that contested liability could require individualized evidence of what sellers read, understood, paid, or earned.

Notice combined email and a linked website, mail for missing or failed email contacts, a press release for unlocated people, and toll-free support. Initial mail went to 20,739 records, followed by mail after 170,746 bounced emails and 16,635 remailings after further tracing. By early May the administrator had handled 615 calls and 975 emails. About 98.57 percent appeared reached directly, without proof of each person’s receipt. The court approved the combined best-practicable plan, not email alone.

sections.title: Fairness and compensation receive separate review
paragraphs: The court weighed merits strength, litigation and certification risks, amount, discovery, counsel, governmental participation, and responses. Dismissed claims and disputed contractual understanding supported compromise. The fund exceeded seventy-one percent of first-renewal fees but represented about nine percent of all disputed renewal fees; neither denominator alone described the whole recovery. Discovery and mediation supported informed negotiation. Ninety-seven exclusions, three objections, and no state attorney-general response to statutory notice favored approval without proving unanimous endorsement.

Because settlement preceded certification, the court separately checked collusion indicators. Fees and representative awards were not settlement conditions; reductions benefited members, and no residue reverted to eBay. It awarded $1.6 million fees, twenty-five percent of the fund, checked against an hours-and-rates calculation over $1.035 million for about 2,600 hours and an approximately 1.6 multiplier. Expenses were $72,923.16. Each representative received $5,000, reduced from $15,000 requested.

The court overruled objections: awards were not conditioned on support, approved out-of-state counsel remained proper, the fee equaled twenty-five percent, and one late objector had no qualifying payment in eBay’s records. On September 15, 2015 it approved the settlement and class, awarded the stated amounts, and directed closure upon judgment. Liability on remaining underlying claims was not established by compromise.
